Many die in the process. Human patients have died from transmitted infections and after their bodies rejected the organs, among other reasons. And health experts warn that this Frankenscience is unlikely to solve the organ shortage. But improvements in our flawed organ donation system will, including advancements in preserving an organ’s function after it’s retrieved from the donor. I retired from a career in designing machinery controls and there are mind numbing jobs people don't need to do, should not be doing and many that people cannot do effectively. 

Look around at the automation in a modern house. I look back to heat the house I grew up in. The coal deliveryman dumped coal into the bin which we fed into the "octopus" furnace, cleaning out and disposing of the ash. You had to stay on top of it and temperature control was inconsistent. My father got tired of it all and had the furnace upgraded to fuel oil. What a relief that was. So many homeowners quit buying coal it brought an end to the careers of delivery drivers. Should I feel guilty about that?

I've designed controls to alleviate mind-numbing, repetitive and sometimes dangerous tasks. Yes, the controls got the job done with fewer people. My work has also prevented serious injuries and saved a few lives. I take pride in that.

But it never occurred how far automation would go. Where will it all end? I'm afraid it won't. And that is truly frightening.

His "to be or not to be" soliloquy is an endless travesty of unearned pauses and pantomimed meaning (he rubs his chest until he says, "Aye, there's the rub" when he *stops rubbing his chest*. Get it?) to convey what his line delivery cannot. What puzzles me the most about Scott's "throw as many elbows into the audience's rib cage as possible" approach is that it's so dismissive of the audience and the text. Shakespeare used to be popular entertainment - actors barnstormed the Old West with their shows and for a long time the deadliest riot in American history was prompted by dueling productions of Macbeth (look up the Astor Place Riots). Illiterate cowboys used to flock to Shakespeare so it's not a question of "elitists" gate keeping iambic pentameter. It's a question of whether you are willing to bring the greatest depth and complexity to your audience or whether you spoon feed them like drooling babies. Audiences deserve more than they get from Scott, which, ironically, means doing less.

Aristocracy is the wrong term. From aristos for "best" in Greek: what are they best at? They are far from Plato's and Aristotle's meaning of best.

A better term is bwana mkupa — big man in Swahili. The big man does what he wants, crude as it may be. And I've read that the ancient Sumerian term which is usually translated into English as "kings" would be more accurately stated as "big men." Because they were often that: big guys who could themselves or have their henchmen beat up anybody they wanted. That temptation by those in power to indulge very basic, very primal impulses is clearly stated in our oldest-known narrative text: The Epic of Gilgamesh. He indulges his whims, beats up and fornicates as he wants. But the wisests of the gods makes a copy of the big man's bad side which he then has to defeat.

And that's the most basic condition for civilization: that those with power defeat with plenty help if necessary what are very primal animal inclinations. And much of civilization's mythos and ethos strives to keep the big men under control — to teach them, nudge or force them if necessary by some means, harsh means if necessary, to distinguish between good and bad, etc. 

We're failing at it.

That still leaves the US absent, giving moral and economic comfort to the fossil fuel deniers.  That issue only gets solved, maybe, in early 2029.  And failing at that point leaves only massive climate catastrophe to jolt the world into common action.   Not something to wish for.  

We may well pass tipping points in the upcoming year, turbocharged as it already is by this huge El Nino.  Let’s hope commercial and local interests can turn the situation around.  But they need support to.  As national debt loads grow heavier and interest rates climb, however, where is the money for electrical grids and generation and other large-scale investments going to come from?

comments.name: The Virginian
comments.body:
In the second half of my legal career, I taught the best legal writers -- appellate lawyers -- how to write better. I offered many key lessons, but the most important might have been, "Page limits are for suckers."

Long briefs are lazy; full stop. Listen to jurists: The #1 complaint they have is that the briefs they see are too long. Give consumers what they crave! A short brief -- Bryan Garner advocates half the page limit, and I think that's wise -- conveys confidence and makes it more likely that the court will read, and maybe even reread, the whole thing. And with short briefs, you don't have to worry about playing cutesy with fonts and spacing.

In my appellate career, with either 35- or 50-page limits, my average brief was 12-14 pages; 20 was the outer limit. Judges love to see briefs like that, and many of them told me so directly.

comments.name: Charles
comments.body:
The point is to communicate clearly and effectively.  Fewer, rather than more, words are usually better at that task. 

In 2025, page limits are dumb.  Courts should (and often do) use word count limits, instead.  This allows litigants to use 14 point type, which most judges, being a bit older, prefer and as much white space as necessary to improve legibility. 

While there are somestupidthings lawyers try to squeeze in under the limits with word counting but usually a little re-writing and some editing will fix the problem.

comments.body: At last, I am a victim of the Y2.026K tech meltdown and victimhood never felt better. I watched and heard about the FAA ground stop for hours on screen from the comfort of my couch, feeling very left out. Imagine how wonderful it felt when yesterday, Delta graciously included me in 4 hours of delays and 3 gate changes in Atlanta. Was anyone getting this on their phone? Reel? Instagram? Was this a Monty Python comedy sketch or a parody of the TV show Rawhide?: 200 exhausted travelers standing around a gate for almost an hour, staring relentlessly at their devices. A message appears on their screens (announcements by a gate attendant 20 feet away being no longer necessary as people do not listen to spoken words unless digitally conveyed). In an instant, the crowded gate becomes a ghost town. A herd of people rounded up by Delta’s app move in mass to another gate. The same scene occurs simultaneously at multiple gates, one herd passing another. Repeat every 30 minutes. Mix in the constant comments of frustrated travelers who think they know more than anyone else and it’s not just maddening, it’s hilarious. In general, do you like traveling during the holidays? Or do you prefer staying home? Why or why not?

Long road trips to my dads side of the family,being able to see family and spend time together makes me very thankful to even be able to see family members I rarely see, and having fun playing family games and just enjoying everyone's presents. There are times where I would like to sit at home and just do nothing during the holidays due to me already going to a bunch of places, like for Christmas, I'm normally at  home with my family to spend time together and do family activities,but I'd still prefer traveling over boredom and sitting  in one place. Thanksgiving is one of the holidays I look up to and can't wait for because I know that traveling will be in the picture and is one of the reasons everyone comes together for family events.

comments.name: ISHOWSPEED
comments.body: If I had to choose my most memorable holiday travel stories I would choose the time me and my entire family had went on a week long beach trip. During this trip there were so many memories to make it memorable I remember it like it was yesterday. The house was huge and we could never get bored. As holidays are coming up as I am not traveling for this Thanksgiving , other than going to my uncle's house which is where all the family goes, This Christmas I was thankfully surprised with a trip to New york city with my best friend . I love to travel during holidays, last then I went on a trip to Puerto Rico with my best friend Jazdell and their were truly so many memories made. I got to learn the culture of different places, what they eat, where the fun spots are, and most of all to make many memorable memories I will hold for a lifetime. I  strongly believe traveling during the Holidays are one of a kind although there  may be crowds, delays, or unexpected turns it always turns out to be enjoyable. During holidays like Christmas or thanksgiving some may prefer to be at home spending time with loved ones and that I do understand because I also think the same, if given the opportunity to go these places with the ones you love most then your set for the most memorable experience.

comments.name: Serenity
comments.body: Thanksgiving is a holiday where I love to spend time with my family, laugh and enjoy some delicious food. Every year when Thanksgiving comes around I usually go with my mom's side of the family. They live in Georgetown, South Carolina, a very small town that a lot of people do not know about. Georgetown is the real country, so the signal is bad, bugs everywhere, in the middle nowhere with small stores a block down. We usually stayed at my great grandma’s house before she died and everyone would come over and eat together. Now we stay at my aunt's house and carry on the tradition. I love spending Thanksgiving there because it is the missing part of my life. Having sleepovers with my cousin, watching Lifetime and the Price is Right with my aunties, and waking up smelling warm breakfast sausage fill my nose. Little memories like these will be in my heart forever. Although this year I am not going anywhere for thanksgiving, I will always remember these memories.

comments.name: Jazmine M
comments.body: During the holidays, I like to travel to see my family. For example, one of the most memorable holiday travels for me when I travel is to go to Florida for Christmas. Christmas to my family is a big celebration, so we all like to meet at my Tias house down in South Florida and hold a really big party that lasts from Christmas Eve and over night to Christmas day. It would be a tradition to play games and eat a big dinner on Christmas Eve, so that when it hits midnight we would all pass around gifts. Some games we would play would be "How fast can you unwrap a gift with mittens" or "Which team made the better gingerbread house". This helped exhaust all kids, which was helpful when trying to keep up their spirits of Santa. Also, the gifts we would give would be separate from the ones that would be at home, those gifts at home would be the ones to open up in the morning when we wake up. My family enjoyed doing things this way because not only did it bring our family together but it gave us a way to appreciate the joy and the blessings of Christmas.

comments.name: Maiya
comments.body: The most recent and most memorable holiday travel story was my 2025 Christmas in Jamaica. My mother and father have been to many Caribbean and South American countries, but have never taken me or my brother on those trips. My mothers best friend, someone I acknowledge as my Aunt Tiff, proposed the trip for both families because her birthday is Christmas Day and she wanted everyone to join her. Graciously, she paid for the flights, hotel, and the tourist experience while we were there. I believe it was a straight, 3-4 hour flight from where I live to Montego Bay, Jamaica. It was my first time traveling to Jamaica and it was beautiful and such an amazing experience. I had loads of fun swimming in the ocean, attending the hotel night parties, and celebrating a loved one. I would certainly love to go back in the near future, and explore more of the culture. After that trip, I can  say that I'd prefer a warm Christmas over a cold one.

comments.name: Zariyah
comments.body: My most memorable holiday travel story is back in the summer of 2023 when my me and my whole side of my mom's family took a trip to Puerto Rico. Everyone got to stay at the same hotel for two weeks straight, which led to us making crazy and cherishing memories. My older cousins and I would stay up late at night and just walk the streets of San Juan, not having a care in the world. I don't get to see my cousins often so this felt like a much needed reunion, even with all the funny mix-ups. My cousin, Charlie, and I were trying to get an uber to a restaurant our families were at,as we were running late, when the driver took up 30 minutes in the opposite direction due to miscommunication. My cousin claimed to know Spanish and accidently told the Uber driver the wrong address, which led to us missing dinner. Rather than not eating, we decided to go get ice cream for dinner and ended up laughing the whole time about the mix up. For Thanksgiving, I will be traveling to Virginia this week to visit my Grandmother and Grandfather on my dads side, which I have not seen for over 2 years. Our plan is to relax at their house while eating and catching up all day, which sounds like heaven to me.

comments.name: Rose
comments.body: Travelling during the holidays is very stressful and fun. At least that's what I've heard; I've never travelled during the holidays. I've always been the type to love travelling; I usually travel during the summer, though, so I've never travelled during a holiday. I honestly prefer staying in my hometown with my family for the holidays; it's way less stressful, and I just get to hang out with my family. I could understand why people would like to travel during the holidays; things such as family living in other states or even countries can be a huge factor, and I'm extremely lucky to have my immediate family live close by. Since I've mentioned traveling during the summer, I would like to clarify that every summer from elementary school to before high school, my grandpa and my grandma, when she was alive, would pick to either travel to see family in Illinois or Alabama. That's really the only consistent traveling I've done. It was always so much fun; the car rides were super long and relaxing. The only other time I've traveled anywhere else was to California during the spring break of my freshman year. I rode a plane for the first time; I liked it a lot, but I don't think I'd ever do it again because I have an intense fear of planes crashing. I remember when I got on my first plane, my mom told the lady who tends to people that it was mine and my little sisters first time flying, and she brought us a huge bag of complimentary snacks. She was nice; she calmed my fears, too.

One foot of sea level rise on the US NE coast caused hurricane Sandy to flood an additional 25 square miles.

One problem with sea level rise is the closer sea level approaches the top of a coastal defense the greater the risk of storm surge breaching the defense as in New Orleans with Hurricane Katrina.

As a result many of our large coastal cities and seaports will not go away slowly with sea level rise but quickly in catastrophic storms.

When the inherently unstable West Antarctic ice sheet disintegrates that's 10 feet of sea level rise globally averaged and over 12 feet in the Northern Hemisphere with its more populated coast.
